pages.text: Archaeologists found 37 people buried in one giant 'death jar' | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Archaeologists found 37 people buried in one giant 'death jar' A newly excavated megalithic container holding skeletal remains in Laos may help finally solve the mystery of the so-called "Plain of Jars." The discovery of bones and other artifacts inside a giant stone jar on the Xieng Khouang Plateau of Laos suggests the megalithic vessel may have served as a communal burial site for centuries. Daniel Baker By Meghie Rodrigues Published July 31, 2026 Located in northern Laos, the Xieng Khouang Plateau is home to one of the world's most puzzling archaeological sites: the Plain of Jars. The name comes from the hundreds of stone “jars” scattered around the area. For nearly a century, archaeologists have pondered their purpose, suspecting they were funerary urns, as some had been found with burnt bones and ashes. Now a team of researchers exploring the site has found a hefty, megalithic stone jar containing the remains of at least 37 people—from a toddler to adults—that dates to more than a thousand years ago. “We were very excited because it was the first time we found non-burnt bones inside a jar,” says Nicholas Skopal , an archaeologist at James Cook University in Australia and lead author of the study, which was published in spring in A ntiquity . The skeletal remains inside the jars were not tossed in randomly, Skopal says, as large bones and skulls were set near the outer edges. pages.text: Ardipithecus: We Meet At Last | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Ardipithecus: We Meet At Last By Carl Zimmer Published October 1, 2009 • 10 min read Meet Ardipithecus . This introduction has been a long time coming. Some 4.4 million years ago, a hominid now known as Ardipithecus ramidus lived in what were then forests in Ethiopia. Fifteen years ago, Tim White of Berkeley and a team of Ethiopian and American scientists published the first account of Ardipithecus , which they had just discovered. But it was just a preliminary report, and White promised more details later, once he and his colleagues had carefully prepared and analyzed all the fossils they had unearthed. “Later,” it turned out, meant 15 years. I’ve mentioned before how unfashionable this slow-cooked style of science can be. But sometimes, it’s the only way to do things right. Getting clues about HIV by observing sick chimpanzees in the wild takes years. And so does reconstructing a fossil–particularly one as delicate as Ardipithecus happened to be. Today, the journal Science has handed many of its pages over to White and his colleagues, who have filled them with lots of details about Ardipithecus , plus a couple excellent articles by writer Ann Gibbons. Ardipithecus has gone from being an enigmatic collection of bones to a new touchstone for our early hominid ancestors. pages.text: Are Humans the Only Species to Drive Others to Extinction? And More Questions From Our Readers Skip to main content Are humans the only species to drive another to extinction? Illustration by Aitch Are humans the only species to drive another to extinction? Tom Ruppel | Dixon, California Human activities are the most prominent cause of species extinction today, but not the only one. A recent study estimated that over half of contemporary extinctions in land vertebrates were caused, at least in part, by invasive species. The domestic cat is among the worst offenders; its cuteness belies how devastatingly effective it is at hunting birds and small mammals. The cat’s influence has been most severe on islands where native species evolved without predators and therefore have no defenses. One can assign humans some of the blame for introducing predators. However, the fossil record shows that species have been going extinct for far longer than humans have been around. Some extinctions were caused by changes in the physical environment, such as the asteroid impact that killed off the dinosaurs (except for birds). However, many other species have gone extinct when nothing dramatic seemed to be happening. Some of these surely were related to the effects of predators, parasites and competitors—though the fossil record generally doesn’t give us enough information to identify the cause of a species’ demise. — Gene Hunt, curator of paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History Why did Grover Cleveland lose his first re-election bid but win again four years later? The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world. Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat. England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically. It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years. It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa. pages.text: Are We Treating PMOS All Wrong? | National Geographic Premium HEALTH Are We Treating PMOS All Wrong? This metabolic syndrome is one of the leading causes of infertility—yet doctors often just tell women to lose weight. Will a new name usher in a new era of care? Doctors have long missed diagnoses of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) in women who didn't have visible ovarian cysts. Experts hope changing its name to Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) will put more diagnostic weight on blood-based biomarkers instead. Cristina Pedrazzini, Science Photo Library/Getty Images By Sabrina Malhi Published September 24, 2026 When Megan Rodriguez was 24, she came to a crossroads with her health. She had gained 40 pounds after getting a birth control injection. That coupled with a flare-up of cystic acne signaled to her that something was wrong. Her gynecologist ran labs showing what they called a hormonal imbalance. But instead of explaining what the imbalance was or how it may have caused her symptoms, the doctor simply told her to lose weight. "Literally doctors just told me that I was fat, and that was it. There was no explanation of what was happening, no explanation of the inflammation beyond just being fat,” says Rodriguez, now 36, from Pittsburgh. Years of specialists followed with more testing and no real answers. But in May 2026, something shifted for people in Rodriguez’s situation. These burros are of North African ancestry. Location: The Black Mountain Herd Management Area (HMA) is in extreme northwestern Arizona, 15 miles west of Kingman. The area parallels the eastern shoreline of the Colorado River for 80 miles, from Hoover Dam south to the Needles Bridge in California. The historic gold mining town of Oatman lies in the center of the southern half of the HMA, along Historic Route 66. Size: Black Mountain is the largest HMA in Arizona, with about 1.1 million acres of Mojave Desert shrub and Grand Canyon desert shrub. Topography/Vegetation: This region is volcanic in origin, resulting in an area that is characterized by large mesas, steep cliffs, slopes, rocky foothills, alluvial fans and sandy washes. The climate is hot, windy and dry, with summertime temperatures exceeding 120 degrees. The winter lows can be 25 degrees. pages.title: Armenia's Long-Distance Trail Runs More Than 500 Miles Past Ancient Monasteries | National Geographic
pages.description: Ongoing improvements to the Transcaucasian Trail mean that the best way to experience the country’s natural beauty and rich cultural history is on foot.
pages.text: Armenia's Long-Distance Trail Runs More Than 500 Miles Past Ancient Monasteries | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Why Armenia Is Becoming an Adventure Traveler’s Dream Destination Ongoing improvements to the Transcaucasian Trail mean that the best way to experience the country’s natural beauty and rich cultural history is on foot. Since 2017, the Transcaucasian Trail has connected Lake Parz, in Dilijan National Park, with the spa town of Dilijan to the west. Anush Babajanyan By Alicia Erickson Published October 20, 2026 Volcanic peaks. Silk Road–era guesthouses. Homemade cheese and apricot brandy after a day of hiking. All of this awaits visitors to the Armenian section of the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), which stretches more than 500 miles from Meghri on the country’s southern border to Lake Arpi National Park in the north, winding through oak forests, deep river gorges, and remote mountain villages. Built largely by volunteers beginning in 2016, the TCT reconnects historic footpaths and shepherds' routes across the Caucasus. When it is completed sometime in the next decade, the trail will span 1,864 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan. New downloadable maps, improved trails and signage, and expanded trekking services rolling out through 2027 will make it easier than ever to explore Armenia on foot. Despite these improvements, many sections of the trail see only a handful of hikers, allowing travelers to wander through dramatic landscapes and remote communities without the crowds. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Arrastra Mountain Wilderness | Arizona View Map In Full Screen The 129,800-acre Arrastra Mountain Wilderness is located in Mohave, Yavapai, and La Paz counties, 100 miles northwest of Phoenix and 70 miles southeast of Kingman, Arizona. This sprawling wildland encompasses imposing landscapes and unique natural features. The Poachie Range, which trends northwest-southeast through the north-central portion of the wilderness, rises to almost 5,000 feet. The gradual southern slopes of the range are interrupted by several isolated volcanic plugs and numerous drainages, several of which have been deeply incised into a bright orange mudstone. The western and southern portions of the wilderness encompass more than 20 miles of the ephemeral Big Sandy and Santa Maria rivers. West of the Big Sandy River, the Artillery Mountains are dominated by the striking red Artillery Peak, a 1,200-foot-tall volcanic plug. The east side of the wilderness contains the uniquely pristine Peoples Canyon. pages.text: Art thief who targeted Edgar Davids is sentenced to jail Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Art thief jailed after targeting Edgar Davids 10 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Metropolitan Police A friend of ex-Premier League star Edgar Davids who stole his £188,000 modern art collection has been jailed in her absence for 28 months. Nabila Habiby, 39, sent multiple works of art belonging to Davids to auction, after he had trusted her to put his possessions into storage during a house move. Ther former Spurs midfielder believed the works were secured in a storage facility in Enfield, north London and only became suspicious when a luxury watch went missing. During sentencing on Wednesday at Wood Green Crown Court, Judge Alexander Jacobs said Habiby, who had failed to turn up for four previous court hearings, had a "streak of dishonesty throughout her relationships with others". He also said she "appears to be someone who thinks nothing of breaching the trust placed in her by people who consider them to be friends". A warrant has been issued for for her arrest and she is now expected to be brought back from Belgium to the UK to serve her sentence. The court heard Habiby, a former wealth manager, "abused her position as a friend to essentially steal".
